items.title: Newton's biggest theorem says integration and differentiation are inverses
items.claim: Define F(x) as the area under f from 0 to x. The derivative of F is f. Define G(x) as an antiderivative of f. Then integral from a to b of f dx = G(b) - G(a). Two operations that look unrelated are inverses.

options.text: Integration (continuous summation) and differentiation (instantaneous rate) seem like different operations — but they undo each other. This is one of the most surprising and powerful results in mathematics

items.reveal:
Two parts:

FTC Part I: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F is differentiable on (a, b) and F'(x) = f(x).

FTC Part II: If f is continuous on [a, b] and G is any antiderivative of f (so G'(x) = f(x)), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = G(b) - G(a).

Geometric intuition for Part I: F(x) is area under the curve up to x. As x increases by a small amount dx, the area increases by approximately f(x) * dx — the height at x times the width dx. So dF/dx = f(x).

Why it's surprising:
- Differentiation computes a LOCAL rate at one point.
- Integration sums up TOTAL accumulated value across a range.
- The connection: knowing the total at every point tells you the rate; knowing the rate everywhere tells you the total.

Applications:
- Definite integrals become easy: find an antiderivative, plug in endpoints, subtract.
- Areas, volumes, work, charge, total amounts of accumulated quantities — all computable via antiderivatives.
- Differential equations: solving f' = g is equivalent to finding an antiderivative of g.

Historical: Newton (~1665) and Leibniz (~1675) both discovered it independently. It's the cornerstone of mathematical physics.

Before the FTC, calculating areas under curves (the 'quadrature problem') was a major mathematical challenge — Archimedes computed parabola areas through laborious limit arguments. After the FTC, antiderivatives reduce the problem to algebra.
items.why: Calculus has two halves that look unrelated. The fundamental theorem reveals they are inverses — the same way logarithm and exponential are inverses. This unification is the most powerful idea in elementary mathematics.

items.title: The angles of a triangle on a globe don't add to 180 degrees
items.claim: Draw a triangle from the North Pole to the equator at 0 degrees longitude, along the equator to 90 degrees longitude, and back to the North Pole. All three angles are 90 degrees. Total: 270.
items.prompt: How can a triangle have 270 degrees?

options.text: On a curved surface, the angle sum exceeds 180 by an amount proportional to the area enclosed (spherical excess); on a sphere of radius R, sum = 180 + (area / R^2) in radians times 180/pi

items.reveal:
On a flat Euclidean plane, the angles of a triangle sum to exactly 180 degrees.

On a sphere (positive curvature), the sum is more than 180. The excess is proportional to the area: Sum - 180 = (Area / R^2) * (180/pi) for a sphere of radius R. The example triangle (pole-equator-equator-pole) covers 1/8 of the Earth's surface — area ~ 6.4 * 10^7 square km — and has excess 90 degrees.

On a hyperbolic plane (negative curvature), the sum is LESS than 180. The deficit is proportional to area.

This is the deepest test of non-Euclidean geometry: by measuring the angle sum of a triangle, you can tell what kind of space you're in.

Gauss attempted to measure the angle sum of a triangle formed by three mountain peaks (Hohenhagen, Brocken, Inselsberg) in 1820s to test whether space itself is Euclidean. He found no measurable deviation from 180, given his instruments' precision.

General relativity: mass curves space-time. Light follows geodesics through curved space-time. Two photons from a distant source, passing on either side of the Sun, converge (negative curvature in tested region's measurement frame). Detected during the 1919 solar eclipse — confirmation of Einstein.
items.why: Triangles seem to obviously sum to 180. They do on flat surfaces. Real Earth navigation, general relativity, and modern cosmology all use non-Euclidean geometry where triangle sums are observably different.

items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.
